questions.why: A verb follows directly, with no other subject, so the pronoun is filling the subject hole: qui. The fast test is simply what comes next.
A new subject (j') appears right after the pronoun, so the hole is the direct object: que. Qui is followed by a verb, que by a subject.

questions.q: Complete: « Le livre ___ tu lis est à moi. »
questions.why: English drops the that in the book you're reading; French never can. Tu is a new subject, so it is que.

questions.q: Which is correct for « the man he loves » ?
questions.why: Que elides to qu' before a vowel. Qui never elides, which is a second way to tell the two apart in writing.

questions.q: « Le jour ___ je l'ai rencontré, il pleuvait. »
questions.why: For time inside a relative clause French uses où, not quand. Quand asks questions and introduces subordinate clauses, but it is not a relative pronoun.

questions.q: Complete: « Le film ___ je parle est français. » (the film I'm talking about)
questions.why: Parler takes de, and dont stands in for any de + something. Decide it from the French verb, never from the English preposition.

questions.q: Which is correct for « the man whose car is red » ?
choices: l'homme dont la voiture est rouge
l'homme dont sa voiture est rouge
l'homme que sa voiture est rouge
l'homme qui la voiture est rouge
questions.why: After dont, French uses the plain article: dont has already supplied the possession, so a possessive on top is wrong.

questions.q: Agreement: « Les pommes que j'ai ___ étaient bonnes. » (manger)
questions.why: Que puts the direct object before the verb, so the participle agrees with it: les pommes is feminine plural, hence -ées.
Où is the relative for place, and it is one word you hear constantly. Note it is not qui or que: no subject or object is missing here.

questions.q: « La table ___ j'ai posé mes clés. » (on which)
questions.why: With a preposition other than de you need lequel, agreeing with the noun: table is feminine, so laquelle. Sur qui would only work for a person.

questions.q: « Le projet ___ je travaille est fini. » (travailler à)
questions.why: Lequel contracts with à: auquel, à laquelle, auxquels, auxquelles. Dont is only for verbs that take de.

questions.q: Complete: « Je ne sais pas ___ tu veux. » (what you want)
questions.why: With no noun to attach to, add ce. Tu is a subject, so the hole is the object: ce que. Ce qui se passe would be the subject version.

questions.q: Build the phrase: the woman whose son works here
questions.why: Whose is dont, and what follows keeps its own article: dont le fils, never dont son fils.

questions.target: la personne avec qui je travaille
questions.why: After a preposition French prefers qui for people and lequel for things: avec qui je travaille, but la table sur laquelle.

questions.q: Give the four-way test for choosing qui, que, dont or où, with one example each.
a: Build the second clause alone and see what is missing. Missing subject → qui (l'homme qui parle). Missing direct object → que (l'homme que j'aime). Missing de + something → dont (le film dont je parle, l'homme dont la voiture est rouge). Missing a place or a time → où (la ville où j'habite, le jour où je l'ai rencontré). Shortcut: qui is followed by a verb, que by a subject.
questions.why: The choice is decided by the grammatical hole, never by whether the noun is a person or a thing. Both qui and que serve people and things alike.

questions.q: Build the phrase: the town where I was born
questions.why: Où covers a missing place or time, and reads as where or when. Que would be wrong: the gap is not an object.

questions.q: Build the sentence: The book I'm talking about is French.
questions.why: Parler de leaves a de-shaped gap, and dont is the pronoun that fills it.
